name: Repetisjon av hele faget
intro: Det viktigste fra alle temaene samlet – fint å gå gjennom før tentamen og eksamen.
sammendrag:
English in-depth study helps you communicate clearly, present ideas, understand songs, improve your writing and act responsibly online. Across the subject, you practise choosing language and methods that suit your purpose, audience and situation.

## Communicating online

Online messages include chats, emails, comments, video calls and game conversations. Before communicating, consider your **purpose** (why you are writing), your **receiver** (who will read or hear it) and the **situation**. Your **register** is how formal or informal your language is. Use contractions, slang and emojis with friends, but choose polite, correct language when writing to a teacher, employer or stranger. A suitable register shows respect and helps the receiver understand.

A formal email usually has a clear **subject line**, a **greeting**, a short introduction, a main message organised into paragraphs, and a polite **closing** with your name. Avoid writing in capital letters only, because it looks like shouting. **Netiquette** means good manners online: be polite, think before posting, and do not share someone else’s pictures or personal information without permission. Online communication may be asynchronous, like email, or synchronous, like a video call. It often has fewer **non-verbal cues**, so jokes and irony can be misunderstood. Messages can be saved and shared, and people may behave differently when they feel anonymous. Communication styles also differ across cultures, so polite phrases such as “Could you …?” can help prevent misunderstandings.

## Presenting your interests

A good presentation starts with planning. **Narrow your topic** so it is specific enough to cover clearly. Think about your **audience**: what they already know and what may interest them. Find good sources, take notes in your own words and decide your **purpose**: to inform, explain, tell a story or persuade.

Organise the presentation into three parts:
- **Introduction**: Use a **hook**, such as a question, surprising fact or short story, and say what you will discuss.
- **Main part**: Present two to four main points in a logical order, with examples, pictures or short clips where useful.
- **Conclusion**: Sum up the main points and finish memorably.

Use **linking words** such as “first”, “however” and “to sum up” to guide the audience. **Visual aids** should support your talk, not replace it: slides work best with a few key words, large readable text, relevant pictures and a consistent design. Practise aloud, use **cue cards** rather than reading a whole manuscript, make eye contact, speak clearly at a suitable pace and pause after important points. Podcasts, videos, blog posts and posters use the same basic principles: know the audience, organise the content and make it engaging.

## Music and lyrics

Songs are texts with content, form and purpose. To understand one, consider its **theme**, the **speaker** in the lyrics, who is being addressed and what message or story it gives. Common themes include love, heartbreak, friendship, identity, growing up, protest and hope.

Notice how the song is built: a **verse** tells the story and changes, a **chorus** repeats the main message, and a **bridge** provides contrast, often near the end. **Rhyme** uses words with the same ending sound; **rhythm** is the beat and flow; **repetition** can make a line memorable and emphasise a message. Songwriters also use literary devices: a **metaphor** says one thing is another, a **simile** compares using “like” or “as”, **alliteration** repeats an initial sound, and **imagery** creates pictures in the mind.

Songs may entertain, express feelings, tell stories, protest or sell something. Music can build mood and tension in films and games, while music in adverts can make products memorable. Genres such as pop, hip hop, rock, country, R&B and electronic music have typical features and can mix. To analyse a song, listen several times and read the lyrics; describe the theme, speaker and message; examine form and language; then discuss purpose and how music and lyrics work together.

## Feedback and revision

Writing is a process, not usually a one-time effort. The stages are **pre-writing** (brainstorming and planning), drafting a first version, getting feedback, **revising**, editing and proofreading, and publishing. The process can also help with presentations and podcasts: plan, rehearse, get feedback and improve.

Useful feedback is specific, kind and helpful. “Two stars and a wish” gives two things that work and one suggestion for improvement. Focus on the text, not the person. When receiving feedback, listen carefully, ask questions if something is unclear, and consider why the reader reacted as they did.

**Revising** means making larger changes to content, structure and language. Check that the message is clear, the structure has an introduction, main part and conclusion, and each paragraph has one main idea. A **topic sentence** presents that idea. Linking words connect ideas, while synonyms and precise verbs and adjectives can make language more varied. **Editing** checks details such as spelling, grammar and punctuation. Check subject–verb agreement (“she goes”), verb tense, capital letters and easily confused words such as their/there/they’re and its/it’s. Reading aloud can help you find mistakes; spell checkers do not catch everything. Digital tools and AI may suggest changes, but you must decide what to use, keep the text your own and follow school rules.

## Privacy, copyright and your online identity

A **digital footprint** is the trail of activity you leave online. An active footprint includes things you post, such as pictures and comments; a passive footprint includes data collected about you, such as your location. Friends, schools, future employers and companies may see or use parts of this information. **Privacy** is your right to control information about yourself. **Personal data** can identify you, including your name, address, phone number, photo or IP address. GDPR gives people in Norway and the EEA rights including seeing data a company holds and asking for it to be deleted.

Protect your privacy with strong, different passwords, two-step verification and privacy settings. Think before sharing personal details or your location, and never share your passwords. Ask for **consent** before posting someone else’s picture or video. Your **online identity** is how you present yourself online; remember that people may show edited highlights rather than their whole lives.

**Copyright** protects original works such as texts, photos, music, films, drawings and games. In Norway it lasts until 70 years after the creator’s death. Quote short parts and **credit** the source, use Creative Commons or free-library works according to their licence terms, or make your own. Using someone else’s words or ideas without saying where they came from is **plagiarism**. Use a source list that gives the author, title, website and date you read the source.

## Sammenhenger i faget

Clear communication depends on purpose and audience, whether you are writing an email, giving a presentation or analysing a song. Planning and structure help audiences follow ideas; feedback and revision help make those ideas clearer. Online communication and digital tools can support sharing and presenting, but they also make privacy, consent, copyright and careful source use important.

## Huskeliste før prøven

- Match your register to the receiver and situation.
- Know the parts of a formal email and the rules of netiquette.
- Narrow presentation topics and use a clear introduction, main part and conclusion.
- Use visual aids to support your talk, and practise speaking clearly.
- Identify a song’s theme, speaker, structure, language devices and purpose.
- Know the difference between revising and editing.
- Check paragraphs, grammar, spelling, punctuation and capital letters.
- Protect personal information and ask for consent before sharing others’ pictures.
- Credit sources, follow licences and avoid plagiarism.

quiz.text: Why can jokes easily be misunderstood online?
options: Because online messages are usually sent in another language
Because websites change jokes into formal language
Because tone of voice and body language are missing
Because jokes are usually shared through email
quiz.explain: Without non-verbal cues, irony can be taken seriously.

quiz.text: Why should you narrow your topic?
options: To make it clearer and easier to cover well
To include more different ideas in the same presentation
To avoid explaining the topic in much detail
To make it easier to fill the speaking time
quiz.explain: A specific topic lets you go deeper in a short time.

options: Sum up the main points and end with a memorable thought
Introduce a new main point and explain it in detail
Repeat the opening word for word and add no final message
Read out the full list of sources without summarising
quiz.explain: A strong ending helps the audience remember your message.

options: It helps you remember every sentence
It helps you control the order of your slides
It helps you connect with the audience
It helps you keep your place in your notes
quiz.explain: Looking at people makes them feel included.

quiz.text: What is the chorus of a song?
options: The verse that develops the story with new details each time
The bridge that links two different sections of the song
The part that repeats the main message and is often the catchiest
The introduction that sets the mood before the lyrics begin
quiz.explain: The chorus is usually what people remember and sing along to.

options: Comparing two things using like or as
Repeating similar sounds at line endings
Saying something is something else
Giving human actions to animals or objects
quiz.explain: “You are my sunshine” describes a person as the sun.

quiz.text: What is the first step when analysing a song?
options: Listen several times and read the lyrics
Choose the song's genre before reading the lyrics
Search for the meaning of unfamiliar words first
Write a conclusion before hearing the whole song
quiz.explain: You need to know the song well before you can analyse it.

quiz.text: What is the difference between revising and editing?

quiz.explain: Revise first, then edit the details.

It helps you replace comments from a reader
quiz.explain: You often hear mistakes that you do not see.

ekstra.explain: Facial expressions and tone of voice are often missing.

An opening that catches the audience's attention
A small card with key words for the speaker
A transition that connects two main points
ekstra.explain: A good hook can be a question, a fact or a short story.

ekstra.text: Songs can be analysed as texts, just like poems.
ekstra.explain: Songs have content, form and purpose.

skriv.text: Explain why a formal email to a teacher should use a different register from a message to a friend. Name two features of a suitable formal email.
skriv.fasit: A formal email to a teacher should use polite, correct language rather than slang or emojis. It should have a clear subject line and greeting, and it should end with a polite closing and the sender’s name.
kriterier: Explains that register changes with the receiver or situation.
Names at least two suitable formal email features.

skriv.text: A student is preparing a presentation about how music is used in games. Describe two things the student could explain about music or songs, and one way to organise the presentation.
skriv.fasit: The student could explain how music builds mood and tension in games and analyse a song’s theme or chorus. The presentation could have an introduction with a hook, a main part with two to four points and a conclusion that sums up the ideas.
kriterier: Gives two relevant points about music, songs or their use in games.
Describes a clear presentation structure.

skriv.text: A student has made a presentation and received the comment, “Your introduction catches my attention because you start with a question.” Explain why this is useful feedback and what the student could do next.
skriv.fasit: The comment is useful because it is specific and explains what works well. The student can consider the feedback, then revise or improve the presentation where needed and practise it again.
kriterier: Identifies the feedback as specific and helpful.
Explains that the student should consider feedback and improve or practise the work.

skriv.text: You want to post a friend’s photo in an online group. What should you do before posting it, and why should you think carefully about the post?
skriv.fasit: I should ask my friend for consent before posting the photo. I should think carefully because online posts can be saved and shared, and they become part of my digital footprint.
kriterier: Says to ask for the friend’s consent.
Explains that the post may be saved or shared or contribute to a lasting digital footprint.

skriv.text: A student is planning a presentation about a favourite hobby for classmates. Describe how the student could make the topic clear and keep the audience interested.
skriv.fasit: The student should narrow the topic and think about what the classmates already know and what may interest them. The presentation could start with a hook, use a few logical main points with examples, and end by summing up the ideas.
kriterier: Mentions narrowing the topic and considering the audience.
Gives at least two appropriate ways to organise or engage the audience.

skriv.text: In the lyric “She runs like the wind,” identify the language device and explain how you know.
skriv.fasit: It is a simile because it compares how she runs with the wind using the word “like”.
kriterier: Identifies the device as a simile.
Explains that it uses “like” to make a comparison.

skriv.text: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence and explain its meaning: “The students forgot ___ books.” Use their, there or they’re.
skriv.fasit: The correct word is “their”: “The students forgot their books.” “Their” shows that the books belong to the students.
kriterier: Chooses “their”.
Explains that it shows belonging to the students.

skriv.text: Explain how a student can use information from a website in a school project without plagiarising.
skriv.fasit: The student should put information into their own words and say where the ideas came from. They should credit the source and include a source list with the author, title, website and date they read it.
kriterier: Explains that sources must be acknowledged and other people’s words or ideas must not be presented as one’s own.
Mentions crediting the source and including source-list information.

skriv.text: In an online school project, a partner from another country replies, “That idea is interesting.” Explain why you might not know exactly what they mean, and write a polite question that could clarify their opinion.
skriv.fasit: It may be unclear because people communicate more directly or indirectly, and online messages do not include tone of voice or facial expressions. I could ask, “Could you tell me what you think works well about the idea?”
kriterier: Forklarer at kommunikasjonsstil eller manglende kroppsspråk og tone kan gjøre budskapet uklart.
Foreslår et høflig spørsmål som ber om en avklaring.

skriv.text: You are making a short podcast about a protest song about climate change. Explain how repetition in the song could emphasise its message, and describe one way to plan or practise the podcast.
skriv.fasit: A repeated chorus could make the song’s message about climate change memorable and emphasise its importance. I would plan the podcast’s main points and practise speaking clearly before recording.
kriterier: Knytter repetisjon, for eksempel et refreng, til en tydeligere eller mer minneverdig beskjed.
Nevner en relevant måte å planlegge eller øve på podcasten.

skriv.text: A student’s draft has ideas in a confusing order and several grammar mistakes. Explain what the student should do when revising and when editing, and which should come first.
skriv.fasit: The student should revise first by improving the order and structure of the ideas. Then they should edit by correcting grammar mistakes.
kriterier: Beskriver revisjon som arbeid med innhold eller struktur.
Beskriver redigering som retting av språkdetaljer og setter revisjon først.

skriv.text: You need to tell a classmate something urgent. Compare sending an email with making a video call, including how quickly you might get a reply and how non-verbal cues differ.
skriv.fasit: An email is asynchronous, so my classmate may reply later. A video call is synchronous and lets us hear tone of voice and see facial expressions, which can help us understand each other.
kriterier: Forklarer forskjellen på asynkron e-post og synkron videosamtale.
Nevner at videosamtaler gir flere nonverbale signaler enn e-post.

skriv.text: You are designing a school poster and want to include a photograph and a line from a song written by someone else. Explain how you can use these works while respecting copyright.
skriv.fasit: I should use a photograph with a suitable Creative Commons licence or from a free image library, and follow its terms. I can quote a short part of the song and credit its creator and source.
kriterier: Nevner bruk av lisensiert eller fritt tilgjengelig bilde, og at lisensvilkårene må følges.
Nevner at et kort sitat skal krediteres.

skriv.text: A new app asks to use your location, and you post a photo of yourself on it. Explain which action creates active data and which may create passive data, and give one way to protect your privacy.
skriv.fasit: Posting the photo creates active data because I share it myself. The app collecting my location can create passive data. I can check the app’s privacy settings or limit location sharing.
kriterier: Skiller mellom et aktivt spor brukeren selv deler og passive data som samles inn, som posisjon.
Nevner et relevant tiltak for å beskytte personvernet.

skriv.text: A joke in an online game chat upsets another player, even though you meant it playfully. Explain why the joke may have been misunderstood and how you could respond using good netiquette.
skriv.fasit: The player could misunderstand the joke because online messages lack tone of voice and facial expressions. I could apologise politely and explain what I meant without blaming the other person.
kriterier: Forklarer at mangel på tonefall eller kroppsspråk kan føre til misforståelser.
Foreslår en høflig og respektfull respons, for eksempel å beklage.

skriv.text: Compare music in a protest song with music in an advert. Explain what each is intended to do and how repetition could help either one achieve its purpose.
skriv.fasit: A protest song can express a message about an issue, while music in an advert can help make a product memorable. Repeating a line or tune can make either message easier to remember.
kriterier: Skiller mellom protestmusikkens budskap og reklamemusikkens mål om å gjøre et produkt minneverdig.
Forklarer at repetisjon kan gjøre budskapet lettere å huske.
